claims_guardrails: No source, no verdict: every on-screen number quoted from ober_roadmap_detailed_report.md.
OBER does four jobs (evidence/blueprint/instrument/positioning), NEVER proof. Cite the direction, never the magnitude as proof.
Engagement != learning is the evidence beat. Show the flat-CTR column beside the separating mastery column. OBER mastery = in-flow quiz performance (add a delayed check).

OBER's winner was FIXED (both personalized arms lost) → the hybrid the authors name as future work = the roadmap. NO learning claim for our own system. Paper named exactly (Askarbekuly et al. 2025, arXiv:2509.18186v1); NamazApp (prayer app).

beats.narration_text: Hello, fellows. One recent study has become the whole justification for this project. But it's a preprint — on a prayer app — with no significance tests. So the honest question: how much weight can one study bear, and how would we know a reading roadmap is any good?

beats.narration_text: Here's the frame. A single study can do four honest jobs — and one it can't. One: evidence — it can test the direction of your bet, not the magnitude. Two: blueprint — a design principle, and the open problem you get to fill. Three: instrument — a cheap way to measure. Four: positioning — where you sit against the alternatives. And the one it can't do: proof. One study is never proof.

beats.narration_text: The study is OBER. Deployed, randomized — about five thousand seven hundred learners, two weeks, three ways to recommend the same lessons: a fixed expert-ordered path, a 'people-like-you' engagement recommender, and a knowledge-based one. Same learners, same content — three orders.

beats.narration_text: Job one, evidence. The engagement recommender won engagement — the most sessions. But the fixed, structured path won mastery — the highest test scores, zero-point-four-six to zero-point-three-nine. And click-through? Flat — about zero-point-three for all three. The metric everyone optimizes couldn't even tell them apart. Clicking wasn't learning — and structure, not engagement, moved it. That's the direction our bet rides on.

beats.narration_text: Job two, the blueprint. Structure first — then personalize inside it. And here's the gift: OBER's winning order was fixed, one-size-for-all, and both personalized versions lost. Its authors name the open problem themselves — marry expert structure with personalization. That hybrid is exactly the roadmap: keep the dependency graph that drove mastery, add the project-level ordering OBER's arms never had. Keep what it rewards, avoid what it warns against, fill what it leaves open.

beats.narration_text: Job three, the instrument — the part to actually take. OBER measures learning without a separate study: put outcomes and quiz items into the data, then read mastery straight from the logs. So our three arms — chapter order, plain search, and the roadmap — get scored on the same signal. With one fix OBER missed: a delayed check days later, so we're measuring learning that lasts, not just the moment.

beats.narration_text: And the job it can't do — proof. This is one preprint, on a prayer app, with no significance tests, and its "mastery" is in-app quizzes, not lasting learning. So it's safe to say the engagement winner wasn't the learning winner — it is not safe to say it proves our system works. It doesn't. We've run no learning study of our own. Yet.

beats.narration_text: So — where it stands. One study, used honestly, does four jobs: it points our direction, hands us a blueprint and the hybrid to fill, gives us a way to measure, and places us against the field. What it never does is prove us right. That's the next study — and now we know how to run it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time the literature "supports" your idea, pin the one study to four jobs: does it test your direction? give you a blueprint and an open problem? hand you an instrument to measure? position you? Then name the job it can't do — proof — and add what it lacks. One paper is a foundation, never a verdict.
